Drip
DRIP
noun (Gen-Z slang)
From English drip, to fall in drops. Hip-hop used dripping for being covered in jewels and expensive clothes ("dripping in diamonds," "dripping with sauce") through the 2000s and 2010s; the noun drip for an impressive outfit went mainstream with rap songs of 2017–2018 (Cardi B’s "Drip," 2018) and then through TikTok and school hallways. The irony a grandparent will catch: in their slang a drip was a dull, wet, boring person.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang drip is a striking outfit — clean sneakers, a jacket that cost too much, a chain, the whole fit — and to "have drip" is to be admired for how you are dressed. The word’s image is luxury so abundant it runs off you. The Christian observation: Scripture is not against clothing well. Joseph’s coat, the priest’s garments "for glory and for beauty," and the bride who "adorneth herself with her jewels" (Isa 61:10) are all in the Book. But Jesus points at a field of wildflowers and says that "even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mat 6:29) — the most expensive drip in history lost to a lily that never shopped. The rich man of Luke 16 "was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day" (Luk 16:19), and the next scene finds him in torment. Paul tells believers what to put on: "bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering" (Col 3:12). A father tells his son: dress like a man who respects himself and the room, and never let your fit carry the weight your character should. The best-dressed man in the Bible is the one God has "covered with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (hip-hop, popularized 2017–2018) for an impressive, expensive outfit or personal style — a wardrobe Scripture places beneath the lilies and the robe of righteousness.

expand to see more

DRIP, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2017–present; hip-hop origin) An impressive outfit or style, especially expensive streetwear and jewelry. "His drip is crazy."

Drippy, adj., well dressed. Dripped out, fully outfitted in costly clothes. "Drip check" — a showing-off of one’s outfit for approval.

Older, opposite sense (20th c.): a drip, a dull, insipid, boring person — what a grandparent means by it.

Webster (1828), root word drip: “DRIP, verb intransitive [&hellip;] 1. To fall in drops; as, water drips from eaves. 2 To have any liquid falling from it in drops; as, a wet garment drips.”

Decode for parents: your teen is being told that what he wears is a verdict on who he is.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:28 — "And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:"

Mat 6:29 — "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."

Luk 16:19 — "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:"

Col 3:12 — "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;"

Isa 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

Modern Corruption

Drip makes clothing a scoreboard and the outfit a verdict on the person; Jesus says the lilies outdress Solomon, and Paul tells the elect to put on mercy, kindness, and meekness.

expand to see more

Clothes have always said something; the trouble with drip is that it makes them say everything. A fit becomes a rank, a brand becomes a credential, and a fourteen-year-old learns to read his classmates by their shoes. James saw the same sorting in the church: the man "with a gold ring, in goodly apparel" given the good seat, and the poor man told to stand. It is the oldest economy in the world, and the rich man of Luke 16 dressed for it every day of his life (Luk 16:19).

Jesus does not answer with rags; He answers with a field. "Consider the lilies" — they toil not, neither do they spin, "and yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mat 6:28–29). The God who dresses grass is the God who has "clothed me with the garments of salvation" (Isa 61:10). Dress well and plainly; then spend the real attention on the wardrobe of Colossians 3:12, which no one can buy and every one can see.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English drip (to fall in drops) → hip-hop dripping in jewels → 2017–2018 drip, an impressive outfit; mid-century drip meant the opposite, a dull person.

expand to see more

Old English dryppan — to fall in drops

Mid-20th c.: a drip, a dull or insipid person

2000s hip-hop: dripping in diamonds, jewels, sauce — luxury running over

2017–2018 rap hits make drip a noun for style

2020s school slang: drip check, dripped out, no drip

Usage

""New Jordans? The drip is unreal.""

"Solomon had the best drip in Israel and still lost to a lily (Mat 6:29)."

"Put on mercy and meekness first; the jacket is optional (Col 3:12)."
